paragraphs: The youth of this era, both Gen Z and Gen Alpha, are often described as the “climate generation,” in part because climate change is already shaping how this generation (which also happens to be my generation) lives and what our futures will look like. Researchers have linked climate change to shifts in where Bangladeshi children live and learn, girls dropping out of school in Kenya during droughts or floods and declining the mental health of students.

But we are also the generation that has learned to push back: taking to the streets, as millions did worldwide during the global climate strikes inspired by Greta Thunberg’ in 2019, and to the courts, where 27 students from the University of the South Pacific launched the campaign that ultimately led to the International Court of Justice’s 2025 climate opinion. At this year’s COP31, the United Nations’ 31st climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, the climate generation was back.

Before the summit, the food and agriculture working group of YOUNGO, the official youth constituency in U.N. climate talks, called for grant-based adaptation finance that young farmers could access directly. The Nov. 19 draft does mention grant-based adaptation finance, but it reserves the “direct access” language for national development banks, not young people.

The one finance decision that appears to have survived the summit is on the loss and damage fund. It calls for the board to “enhance engagement” with the youth and to “take into account their perspectives, as appropriate.”
Did you also spend your free time reading the draft decisions? Email me at [email protected] to share what you noticed in the texts.
On Nov. 19, Higgins said in a video published to the UN Climate Change Facebook account that “farming practices are really under threat from climate change,” the same concern YOUNGO expressed.

articles.title: Summer heat deaths in 2026 reached record high of 5,258 in England
articles.description: Figure for May to September is far higher than previous peak of 2,985 since records began a decade ago
paragraphs: More than 5,200 deaths in England in 2026 were linked to summer heat, the highest provisional annual total since records began a decade ago, according to the UK Health Security Agency.
The government agency said 5,258 deaths were associated with extreme heat between May and September 2026.
The figure is substantially higher than the previous record of 2,985, recorded in 2022, and follows totals of 2,295 in 2023, 1,311 in 2024 and 1,504 last year.

This year’s summer was the hottest on record, bringing record-breaking temperatures and prolonged dry weather. Temperatures reached 38C (100.4F) in Norfolk in June, while a peak of 38.2C was recorded in Gloucestershire in August. England also experienced its driest July on record, with just 7mm of rain.

The greatest number of deaths was during the heatwave between 21 and 28 June, when an estimated 2,401 people died. More than 3,000 heat-associated deaths were recorded across the first two episodes of the season, in May and June.

The agency said the summer had seven “heat episodes” lasting a total of 41 days, the highest number of episodes and heat-episode days since monitoring began in 2016. The June heatwave triggered only the second red heat-health alert ever issued in England.

Dr Ross Thompson, UKHSA’s principal environmental health scientist, said: “Climate change is already affecting people’s health in England, and as the climate continues to warm we can expect periods of extreme heat to become longer, more frequent and more intense.”

“That is why it is vital that individuals, communities, health and care services and local organisations are prepared, not just during a heatwave but in the longer term. The decisions we make now will shape the health impacts people experience in the decades ahead.”

UKHSA said heat early in the summer could be particularly dangerous because people and public services may not yet be prepared. It said heat-health measures should be in place from the start of summer, rather than focused only on the hottest weeks.
articles.lede: More than 5,200 deaths in England in 2026 were linked to summer heat, the highest provisional annual total since records began a decade ago, according to the UK Health Security Agency.

Indigenous communities push back against mining for clean energy
articles.description: At COP31, Indigenous representatives warned that growing demand for lithium and uranium is threatening their lands, water, and rights.
paragraphs: ANTALYA, TURKEY – As representatives of the world’s countries gathered in Antalya, Turkey, to discuss how to accelerate the transition to climate-friendly electric technologies, Indigenous people spoke out against mining on their territories for the raw materials that the tech requires.

“Why can protecting our territories wait, but exploitation cannot? What is really urgent? What is really critical?” asked Djalma Ramalho, a member of the Aranã Caboclo community, a territory in the Jequitinhonha Valley of Brazil.

Ramalho raised this question to the audience gathered at the Indigenous peoples’ pavilion for a panel on mineral extraction. The panel set the tone for Indigenous people’s demands during negotiations at the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change Conference of the Parties, also known as COP31.

Nearly 200 countries attended the recent two-week annual conference to debate an international agreement to limit climate change. Negotiations focused on the goal of rapidly increasing the share of the world’s energy needs that are met with electricity, which can be produced with climate-friendly solar, wind, and nuclear power. The talks broke down over the weekend when major oil-producing nations blocked language about phasing out fossil fuels, which cause climate change.

The push for electrification is accelerating demand for raw materials like lithium, which is used in the batteries that power electric vehicles and provide back-up power for solar panels. Production of uranium, which fuels nuclear power plants, is also rising.

That has big implications for Indigenous people: Fifty-four percent of mining projects for the minerals critical to an energy transition are located on or near Indigenous peoples’ land, according to a 2022 study. According to the World Nuclear Association, the largest-producing uranium mines are in Canada, Namibia, Kazakhstan, and Australia. Over a quarter (29%) of the uranium stemming from these mines is on recognized Indigenous land.

As demand for these materials grows, Indigenous representatives are pushing countries to write their rights into the Just Transition Mechanism, a framework agreed upon in 2025 to coordinate international cooperation, technical assistance, capacity-building, and knowledge-sharing.
Ramalho’s community in the Jequitinhonha Valley has seen firsthand the impacts of lithium extraction. Mines have contaminated waterways and exacerbated water scarcity in an already arid region.

“Our relationship with the water needs to be respected,” Ramalho said in a video produced for COP31. “This is a relationship that goes far beyond the physical. We believe the Jequitinhonha River is a reclining ancestor. Where does my ancestor go when you pollute my river? Where does my ancestor go when you kill my river? When the river has rights, life has a future.”
“They are literally destroying our territory,” Ramalho added. “Whatever the promises of clean energy development, my territory cannot be treated as a sacrifice zone for the world.”
articles.lede: At COP31, Indigenous representatives warned that growing demand for lithium and uranium is threatening their lands, water, and rights.

articles.title: Transmission bottlenecks are holding up wind and solar projects
articles.description: Long waits to connect new energy projects to the grid are slowing the expansion of renewable electricity in the U.S.
paragraphs: Solar and wind farms can help the U.S. meet its rapidly growing demand for electricity. And there are lots of new clean energy projects ready to break ground.
But the country’s transmission infrastructure poses a bottleneck. And energy developers often spend years waiting for approval to connect a project to the grid.

Gramlich: “The big transmission lines that you see when you drive along the highway are what a lot of the large wind, solar, and battery storage developers are trying to connect to, and they connect specifically to substations.”

That’s Rob Gramlich of the consulting firm Grid Strategies. He says before utilities and grid operators greenlight a project, they have to assess whether the grid can handle the added electricity in that location or whether it will require upgrades.
It’s a slow, expensive process with a long backlog. But if passed, a new federal bill would require regulators to shorten it.

And government agencies and grid operators are working to streamline the process – for example, by studying clusters of projects at once, or prioritizing projects in areas with lots of transmission capacity to get them online more quickly.
Gramlich: “The regulations are difficult, the politics are difficult, but we can overcome those things.”
articles.lede: Long waits to connect new energy projects to the grid are slowing the expansion of renewable electricity in the U.S.

El Nino To Kill Half a Million!!
articles.description: Higher temperatures linked to El Nino will very likely save lives overall.
paragraphs: It was once a proud, serious-minded newspaper, but under Axel Springer the Telegraph is rapidly turning into a laughingstock.
Scientists on Tuesday said that El Niño – predicted to be the most intense on record – should be classified as a global health emergency which could kill hundreds of thousands.

“The 2026-27 El Niño is going to cause pandemic-scale mortality,” said Dr Colin Carlson, an assistant professor of epidemiology at Yale University, warning it would be deadlier than the 2009 swine flu pandemic, which killed roughly 284,000 people.

He urged the World Health Organisation to classify the “discrete and deadly event” as a public health emergency of international concern, on par with the Ebola epidemic in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and the circulation of polio.

“An early analysis suggests that nearly half a million deaths will result from extreme heat alone, to say nothing of epidemics of dengue fever, cholera, and other infectious diseases that could also occur in tandem,” Dr Carlson said, in an article in Think Global Health with Prof Christopher Callahan, a climate scientist at Indiana University.

Needless to say, none of these frankly absurd claims are based on real world data; instead, they are worked out from computer models, programmed to assume that death rates increase as temperatures do.

That real world data shows no spikes at all in mortality rates during El Nino years, such as 1998 and 2016. The spike during the pandemic is abundantly clear, a fact which itself makes the Telegraph’s claims of “pandemic-scale mortality” ludicrous.
There was, interestingly, one other, smaller spike in 1994. Chat GPT informs me this was caused by the Rwandan Genocide, during which an estimated 800,000 lost their lives.

A Lancet study in 2021 estimated that there were on average 489,075 heat-related deaths around the world each year between 2000 and 2019, but nearly 4.6 million cold-related ones. In other words, nine times as many cold-related deaths.
You can argue about the numbers, but several other studies support the basic premise that deaths from cold far outweigh those from heat.
articles.lede: Higher temperatures linked to El Nino will very likely save lives overall.

articles.title: As Wildfires Stress Montana’s Insurance Market, the State is Getting Harder to Call Home
articles.description: Buying or maintaining homeowners insurance in fire-prone parts of the state is a mounting challenge, even for residents who have mitigated the hazard.
paragraphs: Montana’s snow-capped mountains, vast forests and open valleys have long attracted people seeking a life close to nature. But that lifestyle is becoming increasingly difficult to afford, or even attain, as the state’s growing wildfire risk spikes homeowners insurance premiums and leaves some home buyers unable to purchase coverage at all.

As wildfire seasons grow longer and more destructive across the American West, insurers are fundamentally changing how they evaluate risk, said James Brown, Montana’s elected state auditor, who also serves as the state’s commissioner of securities and insurance. About 70 percent of the acreage burned by wildfires in Montana since 1888 has burned since 2000, according to the state Legislature. And nearly two-thirds of Montana homes are located within the Wildland-Urban Interface, or WUI, where residential development meets fire-prone forests and grasslands, leaving them vulnerable to wildfires.

“We’re receiving more complaints from homeowners about wildfire insurance than almost any other issue,” said Brown in an interview with Inside Climate News. “People are finding that either their premiums have increased significantly or their policies are not being renewed because companies are reassessing wildfire risk.”

The challenges facing Montana homeowners reflect a broader national trend. An August 2026 report by the National Association of Insurance Commissioners reported that inflation-adjusted homeowners insurance premiums increased between 18.3 percent and 43.3 percent across different U.S. regions from 2018 to 2024. During the same period, insurer-initiated policy nonrenewal rates rose between 96 percent and 216 percent, depending on the region.

Property insurance costs have risen fastest in regions exposed to climate-related hazards, according to the U.S. Treasury Department, and insurers are increasingly declining to renew policies in high-risk areas.

Montana has not experienced the insurance market collapse seen in parts of California and Florida, where major insurers have sharply reduced the new business they take on, but the state’s market is still under great stress.

Campaigners urge Albanese government to reject ‘climate bomb’ coalmine expansion after Cop31
articles.description: Hunter Valley Operations expansion in New South Wales would allow additional 430m tonnes of coal to be extracted and burned
paragraphs: Climate campaigners are urging the Albanese government to heed a “line in the sand” warning on fossil fuels issued by dozens of countries at a UN climate summit and refuse a massive coalmine expansion planned in New South Wales.

A proposed agreement at the Cop31 negotiations in Turkey failed after a list of nations – including European Union members, Panama, the Marshall Islands, Vanuatu, Norway and Belize – said they would not support it unless it included an explicit statement that the world needed to transition away from fossil fuels.
Activists said the government’s position on fossil fuels in a changing world would be soon tested when it decided whether to approve the Hunter Valley Operations expansion.
The project that would extend open-cut mining by 19 years at the site to 2045 and allow an additional 430m tonnes of coal to be extracted and burned.
The companies behind the development, Glencore and Yancoal, estimated it could lead to 800m tonnes of greenhouse gas emissions, mostly when the coal is burned overseas.
The Australian Conservation Foundation (ACF) said it would be “reckless” for the federal environment minister, Murray Watt, to approve the proposal.

“Australia is already one of the world’s largest exporters of climate-heating fossil fuels. What we export as coal and gas comes back as bushfires, floods, heatwaves and droughts,” ACF’s head of advocacy, Gavan McFadzean, said.

The expansion was approved by the New South Wales planning commission in September after it heard from workers, unions, climate organisations, scientists and people around the state who had experienced harm as a result of the climate crisis.
The commission ruled that the climate damage caused by the expansion was “outweighed by its benefits to the Hunter region and NSW”.
articles.lede: Climate campaigners are urging the Albanese government to heed a “line in the sand” warning on fossil fuels issued by dozens of countries at a UN climate summit and refuse a massive coalmine expansion planned in New South Wales.

UCLA study masks energy industry’s environmental gains
articles.description: Studies masking as advocacy may drive clicks, but they don’t drive progress.
paragraphs: A byproduct of living in the Information Age is how easily data spreads without context. A recent UCLA analysis identifying several prominent American energy companies as major methane emitters is a case in point.

The report, released as part of its “STOP methane” project, relied on satellite observations to track methane emissions across three American oil and gas basins, which the authors selected because they “export the most LNG to Europe.” It attempts to link the observable methane emissions from these basins to specific sites and companies operating in those regions.

The authors acknowledge that publicly available data could confidently match fewer than one-third of the identified methane sources to potentially responsible owners. They also concede that even those matches are susceptible to inaccuracies.

These substantial gaps leave UCLA’s report short of a full picture and warrant caution in interpreting its conclusions, particularly when activist organizations use them to make broader claims than the research supports. The report’s inclusion of a “dishonorable mention” list helped it generate catchy headlines and viral social media content. For instance, Greenpeace repurposed UCLA’s claims to discredit Energy Transfer, one of the companies mentioned in the report. Greenpeace, of course, failed to mention that it was found liable for claims including defamation, trespass, nuisance, conspiracy, and tortious interference for its role in the Dakota Access pipeline protests in a suit filed by Energy Transfer, the pipeline’s owner.

The UCLA analysis also overlooks a critical part of the broader picture: increased reliance on natural gas has contributed to the nation’s environmental progress. By failing to account for this contribution, the report risks misleading the public into believing that the energy companies listed are responsible for a disproportionately large share of atmospheric greenhouse gas concentrations.

U.S. energy-related carbon dioxide emissions have declined dramatically since 2005. The Congressional Budget Office has found that carbon dioxide emissions from the electric power sector have declined by about 35% since 2005. This downward trend largely stems from the shift from coal to natural gas for electric power generation. That’s not to say that reducing methane leaks from natural gas wells should not be taken seriously.

Beyond their obligation to environmental stewardship, energy companies have a financial incentive to prevent these leaks. Since methane is the primary component of natural gas, leaks represent lost product that could otherwise be sold. Insufficient pipeline infrastructure, which groups such as Greenpeace oppose, is a well-documented contributor to methane emissions from associated gas flaring, particularly in oil-producing basins where large volumes of natural gas are generated alongside crude oil.

Until that infrastructure is built to capture methane’s economic value, energy companies are taking steps to reduce their emissions. Targa, for example, has replaced gas-powered equipment with new electric compressors where practical. Over the last ten years, even as the company’s processing capacity has grown, these investments in electric compression have helped avoid nearly 25 million metric tons of greenhouse gas emissions, the equivalent of taking 5.8 million cars off the road for a year.
articles.lede: Studies masking as advocacy may drive clicks, but they don’t drive progress.

articles.title: A year of deadly floods and fires – and yet Cop31 still collapsed. When will our leaders grasp the scale of this crisis?
articles.description: Fossil fuel producers are choking off progress while we reap the whirlwind of our inaction. This is what sleepwalking to disaster looks like, says climate academic Bill McGuire
paragraphs: I t’s sometimes said that we are sleepwalking into climate catastrophe. But the reality is that we are walking into it with our eyes wide open, in the full knowledge that we are dooming the lives of our children, and countless generations down the line, to hell on Earth. In the UK, summer temperatures could hit the mid-40s within decades, making extreme drought and harvest failures the norm, and leaving people camping in the streets as houses become overheated death traps. Across Europe, the fastest-heating continent on the planet, the 50C temperature mark could be broken as soon as next year. Elsewhere, by 2050, humid heatwaves could take many thousands of lives in a single day in parts of China, South Asia and the Gulf region.

We continue to pump out the CO 2 weight-equivalent of 800,000 Titanics every year, with no end in sight. Meanwhile the latest climate Cop – the only global initiative with the potential to turn things around – has just collapsed in disarray, unable to get its act together even to agree on a vague form of words about the need to transition away from fossil fuels.

A decade ago there was some hope that we might head off the worst of global heating, when the adoption of the legally binding Paris climate agreement promised to keep the global average temperature rise to below 2C and to pursue efforts to stay this side of 1.5C. Progress is tracked on the basis of so-called nationally determined contributions (NDCs) – in other words, each country’s pledge to reduce emissions which, in the round, should mesh with the agreed temperature limits.

But the world has moved on, and not in a good way. With no binding targets or enforcing mechanisms, NDCs rapidly became decoupled from the temperature goals set in Paris. Today, even if all countries stick to their current emissions reduction policies, it is predicted that the world will still be 2.7C hotter by the century’s end, compared with preindustrial times. This in itself is a catastrophic level of heating that would mean the crossing of key tipping points, including collapse of the Greenland and West Antarctic ice sheets and the likely failure of the Amoc (Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation), bringing bitter winters and baking summer droughts to the UK and northern Europe. But that “if” is doing a lot of heavy lifting, and there is no guarantee that NDCs will not be seriously diluted in the future as green policies are dumped.

So where does this leave us? The answer is in a very bad place. How quickly our world heats up is no longer only about emissions arising from our activities. The hotter the planet gets, the less carbon it is able to soak up; carbon “sinks” such as soils and forests will instead become sources that top up our emissions. Recent research suggests that by 2100, these could help pump up the heat to more than 3C above preindustrial levels.
articles.lede: I t’s sometimes said that we are sleepwalking into climate catastrophe.

New Study: Modern Temps Are Among The Coldest Of The Last 10,000 Years In East Central Europe
articles.description: The modern period may be among the coolest intervals of the last 10,000 years in East Central Europe.
paragraphs: A 2026 study published in Communications Earth & Environment reconstructs 12,000 years of seasonal temperature variability in East-Central Europe (ECE) using fossil pollen records from five mid-altitude sites across the Carpathian Mountains.

The reconstruction reveals contrasting trajectories between summer and winter temperatures following an initial Early Holocene warming phase. Summer temperatures peaked around 7,200 years ago at 1.4°C above the Holocene mean (2.4°C warmer than modern values) before gradually declining toward the present.

Conversely, winter temperatures continued rising throughout the Mid-Holocene to reach a maximum around 2,100 years ago at 1.7°C above the Holocene mean (1.5°C warmer than today) before cooling over the last two millennia.
The modern period may be among the coolest intervals of the last 10,000 years in East Central Europe.

This region has also undergone much faster-than-modern warming and cooling rates. About 8,200 years ago summer temperatures dropped by 2°C over 190 years and winter temperatures fell by 2.4°C over 290 years. Both seasons then experienced rapid recoveries, warming by 2.1°C in summer (1.4°C per century) and 2.3°C in winter (1.53°C per century) over a 150-year span.
articles.lede: The modern period may be among the coolest intervals of the last 10,000 years in East Central Europe.

articles.title: Here's what's next after climate talks collapse: Reform, individual action, hope and more heat
Robert Macfarlane says trust in Cop to deliver change on climate is ‘misplaced’
articles.description: Nature writer reveals in his first Reith lecture that he finds ‘much more hope’ in emerging alliances
paragraphs: We are “misplacing our trust” in the Cop climate summits and their “capacity to deliver consequential change”, according to Robert Macfarlane in this year’s Reith lectures.

In comments recorded before this week’s failure of the 31st UN climate summit to deliver an agreement on action to combat global heating, the bestselling author said he saw “much more hope” in emerging alliances such as the Santa Marta process, which is a smaller group of countries committed to phasing out fossil fuels as soon as possible.

“I would urge us to support these forms of collective reimagining away from ossified institutions that have failed to deliver,” said Macfarlane during the debate that followed his first Reith lecture, which will be broadcast on BBC Radio 4 on 24 November. Diplomats, scientists and activists including Al Gore have called for reform of the Cop’s requirement for a consensus after the failure of this year’s talks.

Inhis lecture, Macfarlane, a professor of literature and environmental humanities at the University of Cambridge whose books, including Underland and Is a River Alive?, explore global environmental crises, argues we must challenge the pervasive but wrong “human superiority complex” in western thinking which has supported centuries of planetary abuse, leading to the entwined climate and extinction crises.

The planetary crisis we are facing is a “crisis of the imagination as well as legislation”, said Macfarlane, because of a “default planetary operating system” that has arisen from Aristotle onwards and promotes the idea that humans are separate from the rest of nature, superior to it, and can thrive by conquering it.

The idea of human superiority spread by Christianity, the philosophers of the Enlightenment and Europeans who colonised other continents is so ubiquitous that it is barely seen by citizens or governments, and is embedded in everyday language, from “livestock” to “natural resources”.

“Governments speak easily of datacentres as critical national infrastructure but don’t seem to recognise that river systems and pollinator populations are also critical national infrastructure,” said Macfarlane.

He told the audience after the first of his four 2026 Reith lectures that the “end-times tech bro” was today’s “most charismatic and frightening contemporary expression” of the human superiority complex, and he criticised “planet B thinking” for promoting the idea of establishing a human colony on Mars.
“It is the ultimate act of consumption and disposal. ‘Hey bro, this planet’s done. Chuck it in the trash, let’s go and find another.’ Mars colonisation is the oligarch’s rapture dream,” he said.
articles.lede: We are “misplacing our trust” in the Cop climate summits and their “capacity to deliver consequential change”, according to Robert Macfarlane in this year’s Reith lectures.

Why the Pacific Northwest Should Not Panic Over a Very Strong El Nino
articles.description: In summary, a very strong El Nino year provides no reason to be alarmed along the West Coast regarding water resources, at least if past "super" El Nino years are a guide.
paragraphs: Some in the traditional media have gone wild about it, with near-apocalyptic predictions of the impacts of the current very strong El Nino.

You have heard the litany of “Super” El Nino problems for the Northwest and California: there will be drought or flooding. Lack of snowpack or excessive snow. That the reservoirs will be emptied or overtopped.

Some forecasts are based on El Niños that are moderate or strong. This does not work because very strong or “super “El Niño events are different animals in terms of their impacts on the Pacific Northwest.
In this blog, I will use the most reliable approach: considering only years with a very strong El Niño: 1982-1984, 1997-1998, and 2015-2016. The true analogs to this year.

In the figures below, green indicates the cumulative precipitation from Sept 1 to June 1 for the very strong El Nino year in question, and purple shows the climatological average values considering all years.
For the 1982-1983 event, cool-season precipitation ended up near normal, with a drier-than-normal November (sounds familiar?), but wetter than normal late winter.
The 1997-1998 very strong El Nino cool season ended up slightly drier than normal after a normal winter.
So, the analogous past very strong El Nino years showed NO tendency for a dry winter in Seattle (or generally anywhere in our region).

The plots below show the observed temperatures (blue) for the winter season, with red indicating extreme highs and light blue showing record lows. The climatological (average) temperature range is indicated by the brown band.
For the 1982-1983 very strong El Nino, temperatures were on the warm side in early autumn, below normal in November and December, and moderately above normal during the rest of the year. Yawn.
articles.lede: In summary, a very strong El Nino year provides no reason to be alarmed along the West Coast regarding water resources, at least if past "super" El Nino years are a guide.

NASA Awards Contract for NOAA’s Near Earth Orbit Network Program
articles.description: NASA, on behalf of the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), has awarded a contract to Northrop Grumman Systems Corporation for the Sounder

Under the contract, Northrop Grumman will provide the design, development, production, testing, and mission support for three SMBA instruments, the next generation of low Earth orbit microwave sounders. The Army had planned to use an emergency provision to proceed despite a now-lifted court-ordered pause on the federal permit authorizing the operation.

Dozens of barrels of volatile lead azide, a material used to make bombs, are stored in bunkers at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown. The Army argues that freezing temperatures will make the crystals even more unstable and the barrels must be disposed of before winter sets in.

articles.title: What’s causing major coastal flooding in California?
articles.description: El Niño, king tides, sea level rise, and a storm could add up to record-breaking conditions.
paragraphs: Coastal flood warnings are flying this week for much of California with the arrival of king tides — the highest tides of the year. The National Weather Service offices in San Diego, Los Angeles, and Eureka are warning that all-time high water records could be broken this week, and the National Weather Service office in San Francisco is forecasting the city’s third-highest water level on record. Already, top-10 all-time water levels were set Monday in San Diego and Los Angeles.
What’s causing the flooding? Typically, the main factors for California include the following, in decreasing order of importance:

Strong winter El Niño events have historically brought the greatest coastal storm damage to the U.S. West Coast. During an El Niño winter, the jet stream is energized, making stronger Pacific storms whose winds can pile up a larger storm surge. The jet stream is also displaced such that more storms are slung directly into the coast of California.

The warm waters that accompany El Niño make the ocean expand, bringing higher sea levels that add to storm surge heights. The warm waters also contribute to heavier rains, and the runoff from these extreme rains can combine with the high storm surges to create a damaging compound flood event.

West Coast storm surges tend to be dominated by the increase in water level driven by lower barometric pressure within the storm: A one-millibar (mb) drop in atmospheric pressure produces about a one-centimeter (0.39-inch) increase in water level rise. Large, damaging winter storms that have brought high water levels to San Francisco have typically had barometric pressure drops on the order of 20-30 mb, corresponding to a storm surge height of 20-30 cm (eight to 12 inches). In order to generate a large wind-driven storm surge, these storms need powerful winds of 20-40 mph (32-64 km/h) out of the south to southeast in order to push waters toward the coast.
Statistics of storm surge (the rise in water above what would normally be expected by astronomically driven tidal fluctuations alone) are not routinely kept for storms along the U.S. West Coast.

High water records are kept of the storm tide, which is the combined effect of storm surge and tidal fluctuations. Since the difference between high and low tide is typically four to five feet in San Francisco, the timing of the arrival of a storm surge matters greatly. The highest storm tide in California’s history is 3.79 feet above high tide recorded in northern California at Crescent City during the infamous January 26-29 storm of 1983. San Francisco, Los Angeles, and San Diego have never seen a storm tide exceeding three feet.

The 1983 mega-storm brought the highest storm tide on record to San Francisco, and top-5 water levels to Seattle, northern California, and much of Oregon. Here’s how the five key factors influencing coastal flooding contributed:

The February 3, 1998, storm brought the highest storm surge on record to San Francisco (3.06 feet), but the associated storm tide does not show up in the top-10 water levels for the city. Los Angeles had a storm surge of 1.6 feet at low tide, followed by a 1.3-foot surge at high tide. San Diego had a storm surge of 1.7 feet at low tide, and 1.4 feet at high tide. paragraphs: The COP31 climate talks in Antalya, Turkey, have failed to reach agreement on a “pact” that lacked clear references to curbing fossil fuels or scaling up climate finance.
The “Antalya pact”, proposed by the joint Turkish-Australian presidency, was rejected in the final hours by the EU, the UK and several climate-vulnerable nations.

With stark divisions preventing agreement on the presidency-led pact, UNFCCC chief Simon Stiell expressed “deep disappointment”, speaking of “scope to improve, modernise and reform” the UN climate process.
Despite a chaotic endgame that saw the overrunning COP become the longest in history, it did not end in complete failure, with many items adopted in the closing plenary.
These included fairly limited or procedural outcomes on a new “ mechanism” for global “ just transitions ”, plus support for countries struck by climate disasters.
There was some progress beyond the negotiations, though, with growing coalitions of nations championing “ roadmaps” for “transitioning away” from fossil fuels.
With the presidency promoting “ electrification” as a key theme, around 80 nations also signed up to a global target of securing 35% of final energy consumption from electricity by 2035.

Cranberry jam: warming winters and extreme weather threaten a traditional holiday fruit
articles.description: Scientists are racing to identify and breed new berry varieties that can thrive on an increasingly warmer planet
paragraphs: It is harvest time in rural Wisconsin, and the Badger state’s most vibrant crop is painting the rolling countryside a brilliant, unmistakable red.

For nearly three decades, Nicole Hansen has been farming cranberries here. Wisconsin produces more than 60% of the nation’s supply. On a crisp fall morning, we waded into a marsh with her to round up the floating harvest.

Cranberries are one of the few fruits native to North America. Contrary to popular belief, they do not grow submerged in water; instead, they thrive on low-lying vines in dry soil. But when harvest time arrives, the growing beds are flooded. Specialized machines shake the fruit loose, and the buoyant berries rise to the surface.

Growing and harvesting cranberries relies on a highly choreographed combination of machines and manual labor, but the process is ultimately driven by Mother Nature. “So we are checking the weather, I don’t know, five to 10 times a day because everything we do is controlled by the weather,” Hansen said.
Across the US, that weather is growing increasingly erratic, due in large part to the human-caused climate crisis.

In cranberry-producing states such as Massachusetts and New Jersey, record-breaking summer heatwaves frequently trigger fruit scalding, in which berries literally bake on the vine before they can be harvested. At the same time, increasingly humid conditions and heavy rainfall during the growing season create stagnant, moisture-rich environments that invite fungal pathogens, resulting in devastating crop rots.

In Wisconsin, the threats often emerge after the harvest is done. To protect the plants from winter’s bitter cold and damaging winds, growers spray water over the vines, building up several inches of ice that act as a natural thermal blanket.
“So if you don’t protect them, they do get cold damage,” Amaya Atucha, a fruit scientist at the University of Wisconsin-Madison, explained.

Atucha spends a lot of time thinking about cranberries and the changing climate affecting them. Data from Climate Central shows that winters in the upper midwest are among the fastest-warming in the nation. Cranberry-growing regions now experience an average of 14 more warm winter days than they did in 1970, triggering erratic cycles of thawing and freezing.

articles.title: Plant-based lunches could cut Australia’s emissions by 15m tonnes, new research shows
articles.description: Nationwide change in lunch habits could cut more climate pollution than grounding every domestic flight
paragraphs: Australians could collectively cut climate pollution by more than 15m tonnes – more than grounding every domestic flight – simply by changing what they eat for lunch.

Nadia Schilling, the executive director of ProVeg Australia, said the findings highlighted the “huge difference” that relatively modest changes, such as a meat-free Monday or a plant-based lunch, could make.
That might mean opting for a black bean burrito, a poké bowl with tofu, or a lunchbox with hummus and fresh vegetables – instead of a cheese and ham wrap – she said.
“We realise that Australians aren’t going to change their diets overnight,” Schilling said. “This is a really practical change where everyone wins. Lunch is a huge missed opportunity.”

Australia has the highest per capita food-related emissions in the world, the report found. It modelled the environmental, health and economic impacts for a range of Australia-wide dietary changes, finding the shift to 100% plant-based meals would cut dietary emissions by two-thirds, while just switching lunches would cut nearly one-third.
Emissions from domestic aviation are about 10m tonnes a year, according to government data.

The organisations behind the report, which promote moving from meat to plant-rich foods and alternative protein sources, called for a national campaign to increase vegetable consumption along with policy and funding support for plant proteins.
Almost one-third of global greenhouse gas emissions are connected to the global food system through land-clearing, raising animals, growing crops, processing, packaging, transport and waste.

The National Health and Medical Research Council (NHMRC) is reviewing the evidence about sustainability and diet as part of the first update of Australian dietary guidelines in more than 13 years. Draft guidelines are expected to be released for public consultation in December 2026.

articles.description: Former US vice-president Al Gore among climate leaders demanding change to consensus rule after Antalya summit
paragraphs: The failure at Cop31 to reach a keystone agreement has exposed the need to reform how the UN’s climate summits make decisions, say international climate diplomacy experts and scientists.

The talks in Antalya, co-chaired by Turkey and Australia, were supposed to agree a sweeping pact that would have injected urgency into calls for climate action around the world and support for countries exposed to the crisis.

But because decisions at summits can only be made by consensus, the “Antalya pact” was stopped in its tracks at the final plenary meeting, after countries became entrenched. Faced with the final draft of the cover decision, many were angry it did not “meet the moment” of the climate crisis, nor even mention the words “fossil fuels” – an omission seen as a sop to petrostates.

The former US vice-president and climate activist Al Gore said the failure at Cop31 was an outrage and significant reform was needed. “World leaders no longer want to settle for the lowest common denominator. They want real action to implement and finance a just transition away from fossil fuels. It has been clear for years that the Cop process is in need of significant reform,” he said.

He said most countries had come to Antalya to move forward “in good faith” and it was “time that we empower those leaders with a reinvigorated multilateral process that reflects the latest science and represents the will of the majority of the world”.

In the moments after the pact died, the Australian climate minister, Chris Bowen, co-chair of Cop31, said: “The fundamental root problem is that when Cops were created, for reasons I understand, it was made consensus only. That’s a very tough ask when you also need consensus to change consensus, which is a particular challenge.” He said there had been at attempt at Cop31 to introduce efficiency reforms.

The UN’s chief climate negotiator, Simon Stiell, defended the consensus-based approach, saying it had succeeded with the 2015 Paris agreement, helping to lower expected global heating at the end of the century from almost 5C to 2.6C. But as the talks wound up, he conceded the consensus system had fallen short in Antalya.
Stiell said he was championing a review process within the UN climate convention to seek external advice on “areas of potential reform”.

Johan Rockström, the director of the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research, said Cops needed to transition from “negotiating promises and commitments that we never deliver on” to a focus on accountability for promises made and their implementation.
articles.lede: The failure at Cop31 to reach a keystone agreement has exposed the need to reform how the UN’s climate summits make decisions, say international climate diplomacy experts and scientists.

articles.title: Colorado ski hill struggles to stay open as winters warm
articles.description: Hoedown Hill was built to make skiing affordable for local families. But increasingly warm winters are making it difficult to keep the slopes open.
paragraphs: The Lind family opened Hoedown Hill to give people in their hometown of Windsor, Colorado, a place to try skiing or snowtubing without breaking the bank. It featured gentle slopes and low-cost lift tickets.
Tyler Lind of the Water Valley Company says they were inspired by his dad’s fond memories of a small local hill with a rope tow.
Lind: “As a child, he would go there and didn’t have a lot of money growing up … and so it was like a dollar a day, and they could go up and down that hill as many times as they want.”
But giving a new generation similar memories has been tough. Since Hoedown Hill opened in January 2024, they’ve struggled with warm winters.
They were optimistic conditions would improve. But last winter, temperatures repeatedly climbed into the sixties.
And this winter, Lind expects a lot of rain because of El Niño, so he says it was too risky to open at all.
Lind: “But my father did not want to give up on this, and so we are keeping all of the equipment, all the infrastructure.”
… and hoping that even as the climate warms, they’ll get some cold winters to keep his dream alive.

How a tiny rare frog became an ecological warning sign for Madagascar
articles.description: The golden mantella is said to be found wherever gold is, making its habitat a target for illegal mining, which is destroying fragile ecosystems across the country
paragraphs: A s Albert Rakotoarisoa emerges from the forest into a clearing in Mangabe reserve in the east of Madagascar, he sees dozens of holes dug in the marshy ground, a sign that people have been here to search for gold.
“I came a couple of weeks ago, and these weren’t here,” he says as he surveys the damage, counting 40 holes. “I’m really disappointed.”

Rakotoarisoa, 52, patrols the area regularly on behalf of a local group of volunteers and Madagasikara Voakajy, an organisation that protects the island’s endemic species and their habitats. He has noticed an increase in illegal artisanal gold mining over the last year, as the price of the precious metal has hit record highs.

Standing on a felled tree branch amid the holes, most of which have filled with water, he remembers this as a former haven for golden mantella frogs, an endangered species that exists only in two or possibly three sites in a small area of Madagascar.
“I haven’t seen any here since 2024,” says Rakotoarisoa. “The golden mantella is a source of pride for me, because I remember my father telling me as a child that it is only found in these parts.”

The size of a fingernail, and coloured a bright red-orange with black eyes, the frog is classed as endangered on the International Union for Conservation of Nature’s red list. There is a Malagasy saying: “ Rehefa misy sahona menc dia misy volamena ”(“Where there is a red frog [the golden mantella], there is gold”).

Its scientific name, Mantella aurantiaca, contains the letters Au, which is also the chemical symbol for gold. Now, the species has become a warning sign of the wider threat that goldmining poses to Madagascar as it destroys the frog’s habitats and populations shrink.

Madagascar, located off the east African coast, is a biodiversity hotspot: approximately 95% of Madagascar’s reptiles, 89% of its plant life and 92% of its mammals exist nowhere else on Earth. The rate of deforestation in the country is alarming. According to Global Nature Watch, from 2001 to 2025, Madagascar lost 5.4m hectares (ha) – 14.5m acres – of tree cover, which is 32% of the tree cover that existed in 2000.

To try to safeguard some of Madagascar’s wildlife and forest cover, the government had created 122 protected areas by 2015. Mangabe, which is also home to 10 species of endangered lemur, stretches over 27,188ha. It is one of five protected areas that have lost half of their forest cover and is classified as critically endangered.

articles.description: Financially, however, Germany spent €5.7 billion on electricity imports while earning just €4.3 billion from exports—a monetary deficit of €1.4 billion.
paragraphs: Germany’s electricity trade deficit soars to 1.4 billion euros as renewables disrupt markets!
Germany’s Apollo News reports on figures from the Federal Statistical Office (Destatis) regarding cross-border electricity trade in the first nine months of 2026.
Between January and September 2026, Germany imported 49.2 terawatt-hours (TWh) of electricity and exported 48.8 TWh, leaving a near-zero net volume import surplus of just 0.4 TWh.
Financially, however, Germany spent €5.7 billion on electricity imports while earning just €4.3 billion from exports—a monetary deficit of €1.4 billion.

Imported electricity averaged €116 per megawatt-hour (MWh) (up nearly 39% year-over-year), roughly one-third higher than the average €87 per MWh earned on exported electricity (up ~20.6% year-over-year).
The top suppliers to Germany were Denmark (11.9 TWh), the Netherlands (8.7 TWh), and France (7.6 TWh).

Apollo News frames this price discrepancy, alongside the headline phrasing about “giving away” power abroad—as a consequence of Germany’s energy transition (Energiewende) and high reliance on weather-dependent wind and solar power, which tends to generate surpluses at lower prices – and at times negative prices – while requiring pricier imports during periods of shortfall.

In the interconnected European grid, electricity flows automatically toward whichever country has higher prices at any given hour. When Germany exports, usually on windy or sunny afternoons when domestic supply exceeds demand, pushing wholesale prices down (averaging €87/MWh in Jan–Sep 2026), neighboring countries like Austria buy this cheap power—often to pump water up into hydro reservoirs.

When Germany imports: Usually on calm, overcast evenings or peak winter demand hours when domestic supply is tight and wholesale prices spike (averaging €116/MWh). Germany buys power back from neighbors (such as Denmark’s wind/transit grid, Dutch gas/offshore wind, or French nuclear) to meet demand. The higher costs enbd up being paid by German consumers.

articles.description: California officials should not mistake a guilty verdict for a permission slip to stop answering questions about what happened between the first flames and the catastrophe six days later.
paragraphs: Jurors cited Rinderknecht’s own testimony as key evidence in convicting him of starting the blaze that grew into the devastating January 2025 fire.
Legal Insurrection readers will recall that I have been following the Palisades Fire disaster from its devastating beginnings through the investigations, lawsuits, and painfully slow recovery.

Now there is a significant development in the criminal case: A jury has found Jonathan Rinderknecht guilty of starting the blaze that became the January 2025 inferno, which killed 12 people, destroyed more than 6,800 structures, and burned over 23,000 acres.

In his first trial, he faced two counts of arson and a third count for timber set afire. After the mistrial, federal prosecutors secured a superseding indictment, charging him with one count of destruction of property by means of fire and one count of arson.

The Palisades Fire, fueled by life-threatening winds and hot conditions, burned more than 23,000 acres of land in the Pacific Palisades, Malibu and the Santa Monica Mountains. According to Cal Fire, 12 people were killed, and more than 6,800 structures were destroyed.
It was fully contained on Jan. 31, 2025 — 24 days after it started. It is the third most destructive fire in state history.

The prosecution’s case traced the catastrophe to the Lachman Fire, ignited on January 1, which investigators determined continued smoldering underground after firefighters suppressed the initial blaze. On January 7, powerful winds helped turn that holdover fire into the firestorm that devastated Pacific Palisades and neighboring communities.

It was the second federal trial for Rinderknecht, who prosecutors alleged set a brush fire early New Year’s Day 2025 that was quickly contained by firefighters, but which continued to smolder and — seven days later — erupted into the Palisades Fire.

“The strongest evidence was the defendant’s own testimony,” one of the jurors, who gave his name as Cameron and who said he initially voted to acquit, told reporters outside the courthouse after the verdict Friday.

The juror said Rinderknecht’s statements about the night in question stood out to him. The juror said Rinderknecht’s said that he was on the hill the night of the first fire, that he didn’t smell a fire or see fireworks, and that it was a clear and calm night.

articles.description: EU, UK and some of developing world object to main text that ‘failed to meet the moment’ and did not mention fossil fuels
paragraphs: The EU, the UK and allies in the developing world rejected what they called an unacceptable deal on the future of the climate, which failed even to mention fossil fuels, in a dramatic finish to the Cop31 UN talks in Turkey.

The proposed deal “failed to meet the moment”, said Ireland’s environment minister, Darragh O’Brien, speaking for the EU. “We will not endorse a decision that does not respond to the science and that actually risks deepening the chasm between global commitments and the action required. [It] does not even mention fossil fuels.”

As the talks, scheduled to end on Friday, dragged on into Sunday afternoon in the longest climate summit ever, it was clear that the “Antalya pact”, drafted by the Turkish and Australian joint presidencies of the summit, would not achieve the consensus needed to pass.

The Antalya pact invites countries to electrify their economies, calls for rich countries to provide finance to the poor to help them adapt to the impacts of the climate crisis, and calls on countries to minimise the “overshoot” of the 1.5C global heating threshold, of the Paris agreement.

But it failed to endorse the “transition away from fossil fuels” that more than 130 countries demanded, and included controversial provisions on “carbon capture and storage” (CCS) technology that some have said perpetuates fossil fuels.

The presidencies avoided outright collapse of the “conference of the parties” by passing decisions on various related matters, including the “just transition” to help workers in high-carbon industries shift to a low-carbon economy.
But Murat Kurum, Turkey’s Cop president, acknowledged there was no agreement on the draft “cover decision” text and so it had not been adopted.

“We have done our utmost; ultimately, we have not imposed this text on anyone, nor have we issued an ultimatum ⁠such as a ‘take it or leave it’ demand,” he said. “It is clear that there are parties in this hall who oppose this text. We recognise ⁠that there is no consensus on this document. Therefore, these decisions have not been adopted.”

Many countries, including the EU, UK and developing countries including small island states and some of the poorest countries, said they could not support the Antalya pact deal, which was supposed to be main outcome of the Cop.

paragraphs: On November 19, Nature ran a research highlight headlined “More tropical cyclones hit peak fury at the worst possible time,” about a recent Geophysical Research Letters paper by Yuxia Fu and Qiaoyan Wu. The highlight in full, as far as the paywall lets anyone read it:
Climate change is creating conditions that pump up the intensity of hurricanes and typhoons just as the storms reach the coast.
Many tropical cyclones are now at their strongest as they move from the sea onto land — a trend probably due to global warming.
The photo with it is captioned “Hurricane Michael was a category 4 storm when it hit Florida in 2018.” The National Hurricane Center upgraded Michael to Category 5 at landfall in April 2019.
I hadn’t read the paper when I saw the title and highlight, and I’m no hurricane specialist. I had an AI analyze the PDF off for a closer look with a note that said,
“First analyze the paper for glaring flaws, likely in changes in observational instruments and resolution over time and how they reconciled this.”

A bit later I added that it might be a small statistical sample. A doubling of an number too small to be considered a trend may be another issue. Both guesses came from just from the headline and the way Nature framed it, and both turned out to be right.

When the flaws of a climate paper can be called from the title, it’s because the genre runs on a familiar sequence, in which better instruments see more, a paper finds the trend the instruments made, the authors call it “consistent with” warming, and a journal’s news desk rounds that up to “probably due to global warming.”

paragraphs: Welcome to day 14 of the Cop31 climate summit. Hope you’ve had some rest. If so, that sets you apart from many of the dwindling number of people at the Antalya Expo Centre, Turkey, where they have been negotiating through the night.
The talks ground to a near halt on Saturday as the co-presidents of the conference from Australia and Turkey held meetings with scores of countries until late evening with little sign of resolution.

The result of that work became public shortly after 3am local time, when the third and – in theory – final draft of an outcome from the meeting was published. Known as the cover decision, it showed signs of how some of the deep divisions between countries could be bridged.

On the need for a “just, orderly and equitable transition away from fossil fuels” – a “red line” for many countries that was absent from the previous draft was published on Thursday – Australia’s Chris Bowen and Turkey’s Murat Kurum have attempted to address the issue by starting the draft with a statement that countries “recall” a previous agreement reached at Cop28 in Dubai three years ago “in its entirety”.

This oblique reference has been added for one reason: the so-called “United Arab Emirates consensus” at Cop28 was the only time that the phrase fossil fuels has appeared in a UN climate cover agreement.

Some countries, notably Saudi Arabia and other oil-rich states, have opposed subsequent attempts to explicitly say the world should move away from fossil fuels. Referring to the Cop28 deal is intended as a way of acknowledging support for transitioning away from fossil fuels without actually using those words.

The latest draft attempts to deal with some other areas of disagreement by removing a hard numerical target for the development of carbon capture, utilisation and storage technology and and acknowledging that as much electrification as possible should be powered by clean energy.
The (hopefully final) plenary is scheduled to kick off at 9am local time. But things have been mostly quiet overnight and it remains unclear how today will play out. Strap yourself in.

Two-Faced Burnham: He Can ‘Electrify Everything’ or Cut Energy Bills, But Not Both
articles.description: Until then, Burnham has two faces, and neither is looking at the electricity bill that ordinary people face.
paragraphs: Last Thursday, Prime Minister Andy Burnham made his debut at the UN climate circus in Antalya. As the first speaker – the only G7 leader to attend the conference – he had five minutes to address a half-empty hall. He recommitted Britain to Net Zero by 2050, declared that “Britain is back” and endorsed Turkey’s pledge to raise electricity’s share of global energy demand from 21% to 35% by 2035 – “35 by 35” – promising a clean electrification road map to match. He even conceded that the “consensus we once enjoyed on science and climate has gone”.

Nine days earlier, the Telegraph reported that the very same government was backing away from the subsidies that make wind and solar power commercially possible. Energy Minister Michael Shanks told a House of Lords committee that next year’s Contracts for Difference (CfD) auction would be paused so the scheme could be reformed. Ministers imposed a moratorium on new levies and policy costs on household bills. And Chancellor John Healey said in the Budget that Labour’s priority is “first and foremost cheaper energy”, which Whitehall sources read as a demotion of the 2030 clean power targets championed by Ed Miliband – who, as Foreign Secretary, was sitting in the Antalya audience.

The same man, in the same fortnight, presents two faces. At home, a Government alarmed by voters’ bills is quietly easing off the subsidies that push those bills up. Abroad, in its folly of global climate leadership, promises to electrify everything faster than anyone else. The two goals collide. Promoting intermittent renewables at the expense of reliable fossil fuels and lowering energy costs are contradictory goals: the first raises prices, so the second requires abandoning the first. Sooner or later, Burnham will have to choose between them.

Start with what actually happened. The headline said “halt”; the reality is a pause. Shanks said the CfD process had given investors valuable certainty, but that Ministers wanted to consider whether more significant changes were needed to make it work for consumers. This year’s auction, Allocation Round 8, is going ahead: the system operator is due to publish its notice of auction on November 19th. Ministers also acknowledged that renewable capacity is growing faster than grid upgrades, causing bottlenecks, wasted power and wind farms being paid large sums to switch off, and said a plan is being drawn up to limit future capacity in Scotland. That is a remarkable admission from a Government that, until a few weeks ago, was telling us that more wind was the route to lower bills.

“Investor certainty” is the polite phrase for the problem. A CfD guarantees a developer a fixed price for its output, and the risk is shifted onto consumers’ electricity bills, as I explained in my critique of an Oxford University report claiming renewables are cheaper than gas. Pausing next year’s auction does nothing about the contracts already signed, which will keep drawing on billpayers for years.

The moratorium on new levies sounds like relief but freezes nothing that already exists, and it sits awkwardly beside the Government’s insistence that it still backs 95% clean electricity by 2030. Treasury Minister Dan Tomlinson has now said it is right that the system costs of all new power are considered. Quite so. They are precisely the costs that levelised-cost (LCOE) comparisons leave out, and which make the ‘cheap renewables’ story a fairy tale. The Treasury’s other favoured trick, moving costs from bills to general taxation, is a shell game: last year’s Budget took about £150 a year off household bills according to the government, but the bill did not vanish; it moved from the meter to the payslip.
articles.lede: Until then, Burnham has two faces, and neither is looking at the electricity bill that ordinary people face.

articles.description: If the past is any guide, a perfect record of failed commitments makes it a pretty safe bet.
paragraphs: Environmental scolds have long embraced predictions, expressed with confidence and certainty. Climate alarmists, a subset of environmentalists, have adopted the same behavior. The problem for both groups is, they often make predictions, in a timeframe, within which their predictions can be proven true or false. History shows they are almost always false, often because they don’t understand how dynamic and adaptive society and markets are to information and scarcity.

The Competitive Enterprise Institute collected a large number, though hardly all, of the failed predictions self-proclaimed experts have made over the past 50 years that were woefully, foolishly, and dangerously (because they did or could have affected policy, investment, and life choice decisions) wrong. In truth, on energy and environment matters, such failed predictions go back more than 100 years, probably longer.
More recently, climate alarmists have a litany of falsified-by-reality predictions, as covered by my colleague Anthony Watts at Watts Up With That.

Some alarmists have seemingly learned their lesson and now make predictions so far out in time that they can’t be falsified in our lifetime – meaning it will be up to our distant descendants to mock them when the predicted disaster fails to materialize.

I’m not a betting man and I rarely am comfortable making predictions because I don’t like to be proven wrong, but I am willing to make a very short- and mid-term prediction, and readers can feel free to send emails calling me out on it if I’m wrong – but I don’t think I will be.

I predict that COP31 will fail in its primary mission of reducing greenhouse gas emissions and preventing climate change. It will even fail in whatever its delegates say its specific mission is – electrifying the world, ending fossil fuel use, getting money for developing countries, whatever. If the past is any guide, a perfect record of failed commitments makes it a pretty safe bet. COP negotiators will hit the final hour scheduled for the conference and still not have an agreement in place. They will extend negotiations, and ultimately hammer out an agreement, hold a press conference, and pat themselves on the back for saving the world from the Apocalypse. However, many at COP31 will leave unsatisfied, saying the agreement is too weak, tepid, with no enforcement mechanisms in place. That’s my short-term prediction. And, concerning the agreement forged, time will show that the parties to the agreement will fail to meet their goals and commitments. That’s my mid-term prediction.
My basis for these predictions is the history of the COP31 process and output, and an understanding of human nature, politics, and economics.
Not a single COP to date has forged a compact, treaty, or agreement that’s goals have been met. Here’s a brief rundown of the COP track record.

In 1992, 165 countries signed the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCC), agreeing to “stabilize greenhouse gas concentrations in the atmosphere.” To do so, 43 industrialized countries agreed to implement voluntary measures to stabilize their greenhouse gas emissions at 1990 levels by the year 2000. They missed that target badly. More than 30 years after the deadline, that goal has gone unmet and carbon dioxide emissions have increased.

articles.title: Una tormenta tropical o subtropical podría formarse frente a Florida este viernes, mientras aumenta la amenaza de inundaciones costeras
articles.description: Una tormenta en desarrollo podría traer lluvias intensas, vientos fuertes y oleaje peligroso a lo largo de la costa este de Estados Unidos este fin de semana, mientras que los vulnerables Outer Banks de Carolina del Norte enfrentan nuevamente el riesgo de inundaciones y erosión costera.
paragraphs: ¡Si pensabas que la temporada de ciclones tropicales ya había terminado, aún no te confíes! La temporada de huracanes continúa activa y una tormenta tropical o subtropical podría formarse en los próximos días, justo al este de Florida. Se han programado vuelos de aviones cazahuracanes para investigar este sistema a partir del mediodía del viernes. El próximo nombre en la lista de tormentas del Atlántico es Kyle.

Las lluvias torrenciales registradas esta semana en el sureste de Florida ya han provocado numerosos problemas, cierres de escuelas, modificaciones en los horarios laborales e innumerables desvíos de tránsito. Muchos vecindarios, incluido Plantation, un suburbio del condado de Broward, han recibido más de 16 pulgadas (406 mm) de lluvia, de las cuales más de un pie (305 mm) cayó entre el martes y las primeras horas del miércoles. Las precipitaciones continuaron en algunas zonas durante la mañana del jueves.

Estas intensas lluvias estuvieron asociadas a un sistema frontal que permanecerá sobre la península de Florida mientras una perturbación atmosférica en niveles medios avanza lentamente hacia el norte a lo largo del frente. Esto provocará lluvias torrenciales en la Costa Espacial de Florida (Space Coast) y a lo largo del corredor de la autopista interestatal I-95, hasta el sureste de Georgia.
Una de las principales incertidumbres es si este sistema logrará intensificarse lo suficiente sobre el océano para organizarse y convertirse en la tormenta tropical o subtropical Kyle.

Las temperaturas oceánicas récord o cercanas a récord frente a la costa este de Florida han contribuido a intensificar las precipitaciones extremas. Los fuertes vientos del este en superficie han transportado aire muy húmedo desde el Atlántico hacia la costa oriental de Florida. Según el Índice de Cambio Oceánico de Climate Central, el cambio climático causado por las actividades humanas hizo que las temperaturas oceánicas cercanas a niveles récord, en aguas situadas a unas 200 millas (322 km) de la costa este de Florida, fueran entre dos y siete veces más probables.

A medida que la perturbación atmosférica en niveles medios continúe desplazándose hacia el norte a lo largo del frente estacionario, podría formarse un sistema de baja presión cerca de la superficie, sobre las aguas inusualmente cálidas para esta época del año, justo al este de Florida. Si el sistema logra fortalecerse, podría convertirse en una tormenta subtropical o tropical mientras avanza hacia el norte-noreste, posiblemente desplazándose muy cerca de la costa sureste de Estados Unidos durante todo el fin de semana.

Uno de los factores que favorecen el posible desarrollo del sistema durante este fin de semana es la corriente cálida del golfo (Gulf Stream). Esta poderosa corriente oceánica transporta aguas tropicales cálidas hacia el norte a través del Atlántico occidental, desde las proximidades de las Bahamas. Las temperaturas de la superficie del mar justo al este de Florida se mantienen entre 80 y 84 °F (27-29 °C), mientras que las aguas mar adentro frente al sureste de Estados Unidos presentan temperaturas de aproximadamente 78 a 82 °F (26-28 °C). Estas temperaturas son más que suficientes para favorecer el desarrollo de una tormenta tropical o subtropical. Otras condiciones ambientales también podrían volverse favorables a partir del viernes, incluida una cizalladura del viento relativamente baja.

Wrong, New York Times, Weather Anecdotes Don’t Add ‘Urgency’ to COP31
articles.description: A chestnut tree blooming in November is not a trend line.
paragraphs: The New York Times (NYT) article, “‘Shocking’ Signs of Climate Change Add Urgency to Latest U.N. Talks,” claims a collection of unusual weather and natural events demonstrates that climate change is accelerating and adds urgency to the COP31 climate negotiations in Turkey. This is grossly misleading because individual weather events, unusual biological observations, and short-term anomalies do not by themselves establish a long-term climate trend, much less demonstrate its cause. The observational record is considerably more complicated than the NYT collection of anecdotes suggests, and ironically, the COP31 negotiators themselves have just stripped language calling for a transition away from fossil fuels from the conference’s latest draft agreement.
The NYT begins with an impressive-sounding collection of natural curiosities framed as “shocking” events.

“Chestnut trees in England that normally bloom in April are flowering in November. Whale sharks that typically stay in tropical waters are swimming off the California coast. And in Zimbabwe, rains that sustain the country’s agriculture have yet to arrive, leading to a drought that is threatening the food supply.”
These events are then presented as evidence of a planet where “warning signs are flashing.”

A tree flowering at an unusual time is an interesting botanical observation. A whale shark swimming farther north than usual is an interesting marine observation. A delayed rainy season is an important weather event, especially for farmers. None of those observations, by itself or collectively, establishes that Earth’s climate system is “spiraling out of control.”

Indeed, the NYT undermines its own narrative later in the article when it acknowledges that “fueling much of the extreme weather at the moment is an extraordinarily powerful El Niño,” which the NYT correctly identifies as a natural climate pattern.

El Niño is not some obscure footnote to current weather. It is one of the most powerful natural drivers of year-to-year global weather variability. The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration reports that the 2026-27 El Niño is expected to strengthen and could rank among the strongest events in the observational record dating to 1950. NOAA specifically reports warmer-than-normal waters extending as far north as San Francisco, precisely the sort of conditions that can send tropical marine species farther north than usual.

Zimbabwe’s situation is similarly revealing. The country’s own meteorological authorities report that the 2026-27 rainy season is occurring during an El Niño and forecast below-normal rainfall across much of the country. Zimbabwe’s Meteorological Services Department explicitly identifies El Niño as one of the climate drivers influencing the season.
In other words, two of the NYT’s headline examples have obvious connections to a powerful natural climate oscillation that is occurring right now.
Yet readers are invited to view them as flashing warning lights for human-caused climate change.
articles.lede: A chestnut tree blooming in November is not a trend line.

‘Hell dorm’: Florida prisoners testify about 119F heat indexes and walls that sweat
articles.description: Temperatures in a concrete facility contributed to one man’s death after he struggled to breathe, prisoners allege
paragraphs: On Tuesday afternoon Dwayne Wilson, 69, a thin Black man dressed in a light gray prison uniform, testified about the stifling heat he experienced in the Dade correctional institute, a concrete state prison south of Miami, Florida, without air conditioning. He removed his glasses and wiped his eyes as he spoke. “It was so hot,” he said, his voice catching. “It’s so hot sometimes you have to put water on the floor just to try to keep cool.”

Wilson said he’s housed in the H dorms, a T-shaped building with one-to-two-person cells, nicknamed “hell dorm” by prisoners because its concrete walls radiate heat absorbed from the sun. The plaintiff’s law firm, the Florida Justice Institute, convinced a judge to allow 31 sensors to be temporarily installed throughout the prison during the summer of 2025. They recorded temperature and humidity levels that Stefano Shiavon, a professor of civil and environmental engineering with expertise in thermal comfort, used to calculate the heat index. He found it to be above 88F (31C) 97% of the time, with the highest heat indexes often recorded at night, including one reading in the H dorm dayroom equivalent to 119F (48C) at 10pm one July day last year. “The walls sweat,” Wilson said. “It’s miserable in the cell at night because, again, it’s so hot. No air comes to the bed we sleep at and the bed is soaked in sweat.”

Wilson is among a group of prisoners who filed a lawsuit against the Florida department of corrections in 2024 for the conditions at the Dade correctional institution, alleging that the extreme heat contributed to four deaths and has subjected prisoners to cruel and unusual punishment. The bench trial began on Monday at a federal courthouse in downtown Miami serving the US district court for the southern district of Florida. The case comes amid growing concern over extreme heat in US prisons, where more than 40 states lack statewide policies requiring prisons to provide air conditioning, even as the climate crisis drives up summer temperatures and increases the risks.

Gary Wheeler, 67, who was also housed in the H dorms at the Dade correctional institute, testified that just months ago he thought he was having a heart attack, but upon going to the medical clinic in the prison he was told by a nurse that he had heat exhaustion. “I am worried about dying. I feel like sometimes when I go to sleep at night I’m not going to wake up in the morning,” he said. “My biggest fear is if I have a heatstroke and I can’t take care of myself, I have to depend on predators who could prey on you because you’re disabled.”

Both Wheeler and Wilson submitted informal grievances to the prison about the heat in the H dorms, some dating back to at least 2019. The men talked about another inmate affected by the heat named James “Jim” Beam, who was 83 years old, wheelchair bound, and had a respiratory condition. “He would breathe like he was gasping for air,” Wheeler said. “Every time he’d breathe he would throw his head back.”

articles.title: Voyager 1 Makes History as It Reaches One Light-Day From Earth
articles.description: There is something wonderfully reassuring about 1970s technology still returning scientific observations from interstellar space nearly half a century later, which is an awesome tribute to American engineering, the ingenuity of the team keeping it alive, and the value of building things that last.
paragraphs: From Voyager’s discoveries to Starship’s spectacular return from orbit, American ingenuity keeps giving us reasons to both look up and look forward.

Over the past six months, I have chronicled an encouraging series of space milestones here at Legal Insurrection, from the successful Starship V3 test in May to July’s satellite deployments and in-space engine relight.

Last week, SpaceX raised the bar again by catching Starship returning from orbit, which is a spectacular advance toward the fully reusable spacecraft needed to make our spacefaring ambitions practical.
Yet the latest historic achievement belongs not to a gleaming new rocket, but to Voyager 1, the remarkably persistent explorer launched in 1977.
Now more than 16 billion miles from Earth, the probe has reached a distance of one light-day, meaning its radio signals need a full 24 hours just to reach home.

NASA’s Voyager 1 probe, launched nearly a half century ago in 1977 to provide the first close-up views of Jupiter, Saturn and their assortment of moons, reached a distance from Earth early Wednesday of one light day — more than 16 billion miles — the farthest any human artifact has ever ventured from the home planet.

Its sister ship Voyager 2, on a different trajectory, added Uranus and Neptune to the outer planets “Grand Tour” before following its sibling out of the solar system and into interstellar space in 2018, six years after Voyager 1.

Both spacecraft continue to beam back data about the magnetic fields, charged particles and plasma waves in the space between the stars as their power steadily declines and their signals grow weaker and weaker.

There is something wonderfully reassuring about 1970s technology still returning scientific observations from interstellar space nearly half a century later, which is an awesome tribute to American engineering, the ingenuity of the team keeping it alive, and the value of building things that last.
The mission was inspired by an astronomical alignment of planets, which allowed spacecraft to fly by the outer planets of the Solar System.
